Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Plasma Exchange for Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome: A Mechanistic Case for an Untested Intervention.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) carries a case fatality rate of 35%–40% and has no approved pharmacologic treatment. Its pathophysiology is rooted in the plasma compartment: cytokines, viral antigens, immune complexes, and platelet‐binding glycoproteins circulate as drivers of immunopathologic endothelial injury, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic depression. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) achieves bulk clearance of plasma‐borne mediators and is established by the American Society for Apheresis (ASFA) for numerous indications that share an analogous mechanistic rationale. This commentary argues that the immunopathology of HPS maps onto the therapeutic targets of TPE, that any intervention would need to be timed to the early cardiopulmonary phase, and that the coagulopathic dimension of the disease provides a mechanistic argument for incorporating plasma into the replacement strategy. We deliberately situate this rationale against the uneven record of TPE in diseases of comparable pathophysiology, in which the intervention has been effective in some settings and without demonstrable benefit in others. The recent Andes virus outbreak aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, which produced a multinational cluster of severe cardiopulmonary cases, prompted us, as transfusion medicine and apheresis physicians, to articulate this hypothesis. We emphasize that these arguments are mechanistic and hypothesis‐generating rather than evidence‐based: no clinical data yet support TPE in HPS, and systematic outcome reporting, ideally through a multicenter case series, would be required before any conclusion about efficacy could be drawn.

Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) achieves bulk clearance of plasma-borne mediators and is established by the American Society for Apheresis (ASFA) for numerous indications that share an analogous mechanistic rationale. This commentary argues that the immunopathology of HPS maps onto the therapeutic targets of TPE, that any intervention would need to be timed to the early cardiopulmonary phase, and that the coagulopathic dimension of the disease provides a mechanistic argument for incorporating plasma into the replacement strategy. We deliberately situate this rationale against the uneven record of TPE in diseases of comparable pathophysiology, in which the intervention has been effective in some settings and without demonstrable benefit in others. The recent Andes virus outbreak aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, which produced a multinational cluster of severe cardiopulmonary cases, prompted us, as transfusion medicine and apheresis physicians, to articulate this hypothesis. We emphasize that these arguments are mechanistic and hypothesis-generating rather than evidence-based: no clinical data yet support TPE in HPS, and systematic outcome reporting, ideally through a multicenter case series, would be required before any conclusion about efficacy could be drawn.

papers.full_text: Plasma Exchange for Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome: A Mechanistic Case for an Untested Intervention ABSTRACT Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) carries a case fatality rate of 35%–40% and has no approved pharmacologic treatment. Its pathophysiology is rooted in the plasma compartment: cytokines, viral antigens, immune complexes, and platelet‐binding glycoproteins circulate as drivers of immunopathologic endothelial injury, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic depression. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) achieves bulk clearance of plasma‐borne mediators and is established by the American Society for Apheresis (ASFA) for numerous indications that share an analogous mechanistic rationale. This commentary argues that the immunopathology of HPS maps onto the therapeutic targets of TPE, that any intervention would need to be timed to the early cardiopulmonary phase, and that the coagulopathic dimension of the disease provides a mechanistic argument for incorporating plasma into the replacement strategy. We deliberately situate this rationale against the uneven record of TPE in diseases of comparable pathophysiology, in which the intervention has been effective in some settings and without demonstrable benefit in others. The recent Andes virus outbreak aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, which produced a multinational cluster of severe cardiopulmonary cases, prompted us, as transfusion medicine and apheresis physicians, to articulate this hypothesis. We emphasize that these arguments are mechanistic and hypothesis‐generating rather than evidence‐based: no clinical data yet support TPE in HPS, and systematic outcome reporting, ideally through a multicenter case series, would be required before any conclusion about efficacy could be drawn. Introduction Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), caused primarily by Sin Nombre virus in North America and Andes virus in South America, remains one of the most lethal respiratory infections encountered in the Western Hemisphere. Since its identification following the 1993 Four Corners outbreak, HPS has been characterized by a case fatality rate approaching 35%–40%, a figure that has not materially improved in three decades despite advances in critical care. No antiviral agent has demonstrated efficacy in controlled trials. Ribavirin, the most extensively studied candidate, failed to reduce mortality in a prospective randomized trial and is not recommended for treatment of established HPS. Management remains entirely supportive: mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure, vasopressors for cardiogenic and distributive shock, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) as a rescue strategy in refractory cases . The persistent gap between the severity of this disease and the poverty of its treatment options invites reexamination of established extracorporeal therapies. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE), a procedure central to transfusion medicine practice and codified in the American Society for Apheresis (ASFA) guidelines for more than 40 indications, has never been formally evaluated or published as a treatment for HPS. This commentary argues that the immunopathology of HPS maps onto the mechanistic rationale for TPE, that the plasma compartment represents a plausible site of actionable pathology, and that the replacement fluid strategy in this context deserves specific attention from a transfusion medicine perspective. We advance these points as a hypothesis to be tested rather than as a recommendation for immediate practice. Two considerations prompted this commentary. The first is mechanistic and is developed below. The second is circumstantial. The 2026 outbreak of Andes virus infection aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, which generated a multinational cluster of hantavirus cardiopulmonary cases with a case fatality ratio within the range historically reported for the disease, returned clinical and public health attention to a syndrome whose therapeutic options have remained essentially static for three decades. We write as transfusion medicine and apheresis physicians rather than as clinicians with first‐hand experience managing HPS, and we are deliberately explicit about that vantage point. Our aim is to frame a mechanistically coherent hypothesis from the perspective of the extracorporeal therapies we practice, so that centers that do encounter these patients, whether in sporadic cases or in the next cluster, are positioned to evaluate and report outcomes systematically. Pathophysiology: The Plasma Compartment as Battlefield Understanding why TPE is mechanistically rational for HPS requires understanding why HPS kills (Figure 1). Hantaviruses infect pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells without inducing direct cytopathic effect. Infected endothelial cells remain architecturally intact; it is the immune response mounted against viral antigens displayed on their surface that destroys the vascular barrier. Cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes, recruited in disproportionate numbers, drive immunopathologic endothelial injury through perforin and granzyme‐mediated mechanisms. The result is not pneumonia in the conventional sense but a diffuse increase in pulmonary vascular permeability, causing protein‐rich fluid to flood the alveolar compartment. The clinical syndrome that follows, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema progressing to refractory hypoxemia within 24–48 h of the cardiopulmonary phase onset, reflects this mechanism precisely. Conceptual rationale for plasma‐directed extracorporeal therapy in hantavirus pulmonary syndrome. TPE and cytokine‐directed extracorporeal therapies are presented as theoretical, hypothesis‐generating approaches; clinical efficacy remains unproven. The cytokine milieu in HPS is the proximate driver of this process. Circulating levels of tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNF‐alpha), interleukin‐6 (IL‐6), interleukin‐10 (IL‐10), and interferon‐gamma are markedly elevated in patients with severe disease, correlating with clinical deterioration. These mediators perpetuate endothelial activation, upregulate adhesion molecule expression, and amplify capillary leak beyond the initial viral trigger. Simultaneously, thrombocytopenia, universally observed in HPS, reflects platelet consumption, impaired thrombopoiesis, and direct binding of hantavirus glycoproteins to platelet integrin alpha‐IIb‐beta‐3. Viral antigens and immune complexes circulate during the acute phase, potentially sustaining toll‐like receptor and innate immune activation even as viremia begins to clear. The myocardial depression characteristic of HPS adds a cardiogenic component to what is otherwise a distributive and permeability‐driven shock syndrome. Depressed left ventricular ejection fraction in the acute phase is well described and reflects the effects of circulating mediators on myocardial contractility rather than ischemia or direct viral invasion. This low cardiac output state, superimposed on alveolar flooding from capillary leak, produces the particularly lethal hemodynamic phenotype that distinguishes HPS from other viral pneumonias and has prompted the preferred designation hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). The central observation for the transfusion medicine audience is this: the pathogenic burden in HPS is not primarily cellular or structural. It is humoral. Cytokines, viral antigens, immune complexes, activated complement fragments, and dysfunctional platelet‐binding viral glycoproteins all circulate in plasma. The plasma compartment is both the propagation medium and the therapeutic target. Mechanistic Rationale for Therapeutic Plasma Exchange TPE removes one to one and a half plasma volumes per session, clearing approximately 63%–78% of any given plasma constituent in a single procedure. In diseases characterized by pathogenic circulating mediators, this degree of bulk clearance exceeds what pharmacologic suppression or renal replacement therapy can achieve on a comparable timescale. The ASFA guidelines assign Category I or II designations to disorders spanning autoimmune, hematologic, and neurologic disease on exactly this basis. Applied to HPS, TPE would be expected to achieve several mechanistic objectives simultaneously. Cytokine clearance is the most immediate rationale. TNF‐alpha, IL‐6, and interferon‐gamma are predominantly plasma‐borne mediators in the molecular weight range of 17 to 26 kDa, well within the clearance profile of centrifugal plasma separation. A single 1.0 plasma volume exchange reduces circulating cytokine levels by approximately 50 to 65% before endogenous resynthesis begins. In a disease where the severity and duration of the cytokine storm directly predict mortality, even a transient reduction in circulating mediator burden could plausibly interrupt the immunopathologic cascade before irreversible lung injury is fully established. This therapeutic window, corresponding roughly to Days 4–8 of illness when the cardiopulmonary phase begins, is when any intervention would need to be timed. Viral antigen and immune complex removal represents a distinct and complementary rationale. Hantavirus nucleocapsid antigen and glycoprotein fragments circulate during the acute viremic phase, potentially sustaining innate immune activation through pattern recognition receptor engagement. Immune complexes formed between viral antigens and early antibody responses can deposit in vascular beds and amplify complement‐mediated endothelial injury. TPE removes both the antigen burden and the complexes formed against it, reducing the substrate for ongoing complement activation. Restoration of ADAMTS13 and endothelial‐protective proteins is a mechanism that has received insufficient attention in the emerging infection literature but is relevant here. Severe inflammatory states consume ADAMTS13, the von Willebrand factor‐cleaving protease whose deficiency underlies thrombotic microangiopathy. Whether HPS is accompanied by clinically significant ADAMTS13 depletion has not been formally studied, but the consumptive coagulopathy and platelet dysfunction observed in the disease create a phenotype that could benefit from restoration of this and other regulatory plasma proteins. Replacement Fluid Strategy: A Transfusion Medicine Perspective The choice of replacement fluid in TPE for HPS deserves specific consideration and distinguishes this hypothetical indication from the majority of ASFA‐guided diseases in which albumin alone suffices. In most established indications, albumin replacement is preferred because it avoids the infectious and allergic risks associated with plasma products and adequately restores oncotic pressure. In HPS, however, the coagulopathic dimension of the disease argues for a different calculus. Patients in the cardiopulmonary phase of HPS frequently exhibit prolonged prothrombin times, elevated fibrin degradation products, and reduced fibrinogen, reflecting a consumptive coagulopathic process superimposed on severe thrombocytopenia. In this setting, albumin‐only replacement across serial exchanges would be expected to accelerate depletion of residual coagulation factors by dilution, potentially worsening an already compromised hemostatic capacity. This concern provides a mechanistic argument for using plasma for all or a substantial portion of the exchange volume in HPS. We stress, however, that this remains a mechanistic argument and not an evidence‐based one: albumin replacement has not been shown to be ineffective or harmful in HPS, no comparative data exist, and the choice of replacement fluid in any individual patient must weigh the theoretical hemostatic benefit of plasma against its infectious, allergic, and TRALI‐associated risks. Beyond coagulation factor repletion, plasma provides alpha‐2‐macroglobulin (a broad‐spectrum protease inhibitor and cytokine carrier), protein C and antithrombin (anti‐inflammatory and anticoagulant mediators consumed during critical illness), and endothelial‐protective proteins that are stripped away by the inflammatory milieu. This argument parallels the rationale for plasma replacement in TPE for thrombotic microangiopathy, where ADAMTS13 repletion is the explicit therapeutic goal. In HPS, the goal would be broader, but the logic is analogous: replace what the disease process has consumed while simultaneously removing what it has generated in excess. The strength of this analogy, however, should not be overstated in the absence of any HPS‐specific data. Practical considerations regarding ABO compatibility and the risk of transfusion‐related acute lung injury (TRALI) in a patient with already‐compromised pulmonary reserve require careful attention and close coordination between the apheresis service and the intensive care unit. Because the residual risk of transfusion‐transmitted viral infection from modern plasma products is already very low, the incremental safety benefit of pathogen‐reduced plasma in this context is modest; where such products are available, however, they may offer an additional margin of safety that is reasonable to prefer given the setting of active viral infection. The volume dynamics of a 1.0–1.5 plasma volume exchange in a hemodynamically unstable patient with diminished cardiac reserve mandate continuous hemodynamic monitoring throughout the procedure and may require vasopressor support during the exchange itself. Alternative Extracorporeal Strategies: Cytokine Adsorption and Hemofiltration TPE is not the only extracorporeal option capable of lowering the circulating mediator burden in HPS, and any argument for it must account for the alternatives. Selective cytokine adsorption columns, such as those incorporating porous polymer beads, and high‐volume hemofiltration both reduce plasma cytokine concentrations and have been described in cytokine‐driven critical illness, including a reported case of hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome treated with high‐volume hemofiltration. These modalities carry real advantages in the coagulopathic HPS patient: they do not require large volumes of plasma, they avoid the transfusion exposure and TRALI risk inherent to plasma replacement, and adsorption can often be integrated into an existing continuous renal replacement circuit. Their principal limitation relative to TPE is that they are subtractive only. Adsorption and hemofiltration remove cytokines within a defined size range but do not efficiently clear larger immune complexes and do not replete the regulatory and hemostatic plasma proteins that the disease consumes. TPE is distinctive precisely because it couples broad removal with simultaneous restoration of plasma composition, the feature most relevant to the consumptive coagulopathy of HPS. We do not regard these approaches as mutually exclusive; in a given patient, adsorption, hemofiltration, and TPE could prove complementary, and the relative merits of each remain entirely untested in this disease. Precedent and Positioning TPE has not been used for HPS in any published report, but extracorporeal cytokine removal has. High‐volume continuous hemofiltration (HVHF) was applied to a patient with HCPS and refractory cardiogenic shock in a 2016 Chilean case report, with hemodynamic improvement within hours of initiation. The authors attributed the benefit specifically to cytokine clearance across the hemofilter membrane. If cytokine removal via CRRT can influence the HPS shock state, the case for TPE, which achieves cytokine clearance with greater efficiency per unit time and simultaneously restores plasma protein composition, is at least worth examining. A single case report, however, cannot establish efficacy for either modality. Convalescent plasma has also been examined in the HPS context, with a small interventional study demonstrating a borderline‐significant reduction in case fatality rate when administered early in the viremic phase. Convalescent plasma and TPE are mechanistically distinct: the former provides neutralizing antibodies against viral antigens, the latter removes pathogenic circulating mediators. They could in principle be complementary in a sequential protocol, with TPE addressing the immunopathologic phase and convalescent plasma targeting viremia in the days preceding it. The analogy to antibody replacement following TPE in myasthenia gravis is imperfect but instructive. More broadly, TPE has been applied to cytokine‐storm syndromes of diverse etiology including hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, macrophage activation syndrome, and severe COVID‐19, where the pathophysiology shares important features with HPS: immunopathologic endothelial injury, consumptive coagulopathy, and cytokine‐driven organ failure. The mechanistic parallels support extrapolation of the TPE rationale to HPS, while acknowledging that the viral trigger and the specific immune effector populations differ. This mechanistic optimism must be tempered by the uneven record of TPE across diseases whose pathophysiology superficially resembles that of HPS, because plausibility has repeatedly failed to predict benefit. On the favorable side, TPE is unambiguously life‐saving in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, and it has produced apparent benefit in selected reports of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, macrophage activation syndrome, and catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome, all disorders defined by circulating mediators and endothelial injury. On the unfavorable side, sepsis and septic shock, the archetypal cytokine‐storm and endothelial‐injury syndrome, illustrate the opposite lesson. Despite a mechanistic rationale essentially identical to the one advanced here, and despite a small randomized trial suggesting a mortality reduction, the broader evidence for TPE in adult sepsis remains insufficient to establish benefit, and the intervention is not part of standard management. papers.title: Detection of new world hantaviruses by a broadly reactive rRT-PCR assay.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Orthohantaviruses are negative-sense RNA viruses that persistently infect rodents and can cause severe human disease. Orthohantavirus diversity complicates comprehensive surveillance strategies and diagnostic tools. Currently, serological assays and nested PCR with degenerate primers are used for hantavirus diagnosis and rodent surveillance, but these assays have long turnaround-times. Here, a broadly reactive Orthohantavirus real-time PCR assay is presented that can be incorporated into public health and research laboratories across the Americas. STUDY DESIGN: Starting from an existing rRT-PCR primer-probe set originally developed for the detection of Sin Nombre virus, a pan-America Orthohantavirus assay (HantAmeriQ) was developed that can be used for both human and rodent surveillance. RESULTS: Using synthetic RNA, the HantAmeriQ assay detected all New World Orthohantaviruses known to cause human disease at a limit of detection between 25 (Blue River virus) and 28,000 (Bayou virus) copies/reaction. Genetically diverse hantaviruses from North America (including Sin Nombre, New York, Monongahela, Blue River, and Bayou viruses) and Central/South America (including Catacamas, Carrizal, Choclo, Maciel, and Andes viruses) were detected within similar limits. The HantAmeriQ assay performed as well as or better than a commercially available assay for the detection of North American, but not South American hantaviruses and detected diverse hantaviruses from rodent and human specimens. CONCLUSIONS: Here, the HantAmeriQ assay detected New World Orthohantaviruses in both rodent and human samples from across the United States, and hantaviruses from Central and South America. The assay demonstrates strong potential for diagnostic use in North American clinical laboratories and for surveillance and research applications in rodent-centered field studies.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence for chest imaging in hantavirus pulmonary syndrome: A review of practical considerations for rare-disease imaging.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) is an uncommon zoonotic respiratory illness with a high case fatality rate. Recent travel-associated Andes orthohantavirus clusters have renewed interest in early radiographic recognition of the disease outside its usual geographic range. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools developed during the COVID-19 pandemic now inform several radiology workflows, but the application of AI to HPS chest imaging remains largely unexplored. This narrative review summarises the imaging features of HPS across modalities, considers lessons from AI applications in COVID-19 and viral pneumonia imaging, and discusses practical development considerations for HPS-aware imaging AI, including dataset development, label standardisation, realistic comparator inclusion, candidate modelling approaches, external validation, and clinical workflow integration. The review also considers challenges to HPS-aware imaging AI, including data scarcity, low pretest probability in non-endemic settings, overlapping imaging findings, and translational pitfalls from recent AI literature. As HPS is unlikely to support conventional disease-specific model development without coordinated data collection, future work will likely require multi-institutional datasets, prevalence-aware evaluation, and multimodal workflow integration that combines imaging with clinical, laboratory, and epidemiologic context.

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒肺综合征是一种罕见的动物源性呼吸系统疾病,致死率高,近期与旅行相关的安第斯病毒 正汉坦病毒 簇再次引起了对在非流行地区早期影像学识别的关注。

papers.title: Use of tocilizumab for severe hantavirus pulmonary syndrome: a MEURI case series with contextual comparisons.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome is a rare zoonotic disease associated with high mortality, acute respiratory failure, shock, capillary leak, and systemic inflammation. Currently, no specific antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has proven effective for routine clinical use. The current cruise-associated hantavirus outbreak motivated this early descriptive report from an ongoing, larger, pre-post study (ISRCTN72088243). We aimed to describe tocilizumab use under the Monitored Emergency Use of Unregistered and Investigational Interventions (MEURI) framework. METHODS: In this descriptive case series at Hospital Zonal de Bariloche Dr Ramón Carrillo, San Carlos de Bariloche, Argentina, patients with laboratory-confirmed severe hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission or assessment were eligible to receive tocilizumab in addition to standard supportive care, in accordance with the MEURI framework. Tocilizumab was administered to patients within 24 h of ICU admission or ICU-level evaluation as a single intravenous dose of 8 mg/kg, up to a maximum of 800 mg. During this time, five eligible patients could not receive tocilizumab because timely administration was not feasible due to drug unavailability or refractory shock at diagnosis. This case series represents the first report from the larger, ongoing, pre-post study (ISRCTN72088243). The main descriptive outcome was survival to ICU discharge in patients who received tocilizumab and patients who were eligible to receive tocilizumab but did not. FINDINGS: Between June 1, 2024, and May 5, 2026, 13 patients with laboratory-confirmed hantavirus pulmonary syndrome were evaluated for inclusion after institutional approval of the MEURI protocol. Ten met eligibility criteria for tocilizumab; five received tocilizumab and five did not. In the five eligible non-treated patients, two were diagnosed when they were already in refractory shock, precluding timely administration, and three did not receive tocilizumab because the drug was unavailable when treatment was being considered. Four of five tocilizumab-treated patients survived to ICU discharge. The fifth treated patient died after rapid progression to refractory shock. All five eligible non-treated patients died after ICU admission. INTERPRETATION: These observations suggest that IL-6 inhibition warrants further evaluation within the MEURI framework or analogous expanded-access frameworks, and, when feasible, collaborative randomised studies with standardised data collection. FUNDING: None. TRANSLATIONS: For the Spanish translations of the abstract see Supplementary Materials section.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome is a rare, high‑mortality zoonosis with severe respiratory and systemic effects, and no proven specific therapy (A1, A2). Methods: In Argentina, a descriptive case series under the MEURI framework enrolled severe, ICU‑eligible HPS patients, administering a single 8 mg/kg IV dose of tocilizumab within 24 h; 13 were evaluated, 10 eligible, five treated, five untreated (A5‑A12). Results: Four of five treated patients survived ICU discharge, one died; all five untreated patients died (A14‑A16). Contribution: The findings suggest IL‑6 inhibition merits further study in expanded‑access or randomised trials (A17). Limitations: Only the abstract is provided, limiting methodological detail and statistical power due to the small sample size.

papers.title_zh: 托珠单抗用于重症汉坦病毒肺综合征的研究:MEURI病例系列及情境比较。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒肺综合征 是一种罕见的动物源性疾病,死亡率高,表现为急性呼吸衰竭、休克、毛细血管渗漏和全身炎症 (A1)。目前尚无特异性抗病毒或免疫调节治疗被证实可常规使用 (A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 在阿根廷巴里洛切地区医院开展了一项描述性病例系列研究,纳入实验室确诊的重症汉坦病毒肺综合征患者,需入住ICU (A5)。托珠单抗在ICU入院后24小时内以单次静脉注射 8 mg/kg(最高 800 mg)给药 (A6)。2024年6月1日至2026年5月5日期间,共评估13例患者;其中10例符合入选标准,5例接受托珠单抗治疗,5例未接受 (A10‐A12)。
analysis_zh.results: 5例接受托珠单抗治疗的患者中有4例存活至ICU出院,1例因快速进展为难治性休克而死亡 (A14‐A15)。所有5例符合条件的未治疗患者在ICU入院后均死亡 (A16)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 作者将此观察解读为 IL‐6 抑制值得在 MEURI 或类似的扩展使用框架以及合作随机研究中进一步评估 (A17)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅有摘要可得,导致研究设计、患者特征和统计分析细节受限;样本量过小,无法得出明确的疗效结论。

papers.title: Hantavirus risk and preparedness in Europe in an era of climate change and global mobility.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonoses causing haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. In Europe, Puumala virus (PUUV) and Dobrava virus (DOBV) account for most recognized disease; Seoul virus (SEOV) is relevant to ports and urban settings. The 2026 MV Hondius cruise-ship cluster of Andes hantavirus (ANDV) infections, involving passengers from 23 countries, has highlighted urgent gaps in European preparedness for both endemic and imported hantavirus disease. OBJECTIVES: To review hantavirus epidemiology, ecology, clinical recognition, diagnostics, and preparedness in Europe, with emphasis on endemic PUUV, DOBV, and SEOV, and to clarify the separate relevance of imported ANDV infection for travel medicine and maritime response. SOURCES: We conducted a structured narrative review of literature published from January 2000 to May 2026, prioritizing surveillance reports, systematic and narrative reviews, rodent ecology studies, diagnostic evaluations, external quality assessment studies, and outbreak investigations. WHO, European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, and International Health Regulations guidance documents were also reviewed. CONTENT: European hantavirus epidemiology is heterogeneous and shaped by reservoir ecology, biome-specific rodent dynamics, clinical awareness, diagnostic capacity, and surveillance practice. Climate effects are indirect and regionally variable, mediated by mast years, predator-prey dynamics, winter conditions, land use, reservoir density, and human exposure. Diagnostic preparedness is uneven, particularly for molecular detection. Imported ANDV infection is rare in Europe but relevant to travel medicine and high-consequence preparedness because it can cause severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and, unlike endemic European hantaviruses, has documented person-to-person transmission. IMPLICATIONS: European preparedness should prioritize PUUV, DOBV, and SEOV through rodent biomonitoring, harmonized surveillance, improved molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early warning.
papers.journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonoses causing haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, and the 2026 MV Hondius cruise‑ship Andes virus outbreak highlighted urgent gaps in European preparedness.
analysis.main_directions: The review examines European epidemiology of PUUV, DOBV and SEOV, clinical recognition, diagnostics, surveillance, and the distinct travel‑medicine relevance of imported ANDV infection.
analysis.current_state: European hantavirus risk is heterogeneous, driven by reservoir ecology, climate‑mediated rodent dynamics, and variable diagnostic capacity across countries.
analysis.gaps: The cruise‑ship cluster exposed critical deficiencies in coordinated response, and molecular diagnostic preparedness remains uneven.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonoses causing HFRS and HPS, and a 2026 cruise‑ship Andes virus outbreak highlighted preparedness gaps in Europe. Main directions: The review addresses European epidemiology of PUUV, DOBV and SEOV, clinical recognition, diagnostics, surveillance, and the travel‑medicine relevance of imported ANDV. Current state: Risk is heterogeneous, shaped by reservoir ecology, climate‑driven rodent dynamics, and uneven diagnostic capacity. Gaps: The cruise‑ship cluster exposed critical response deficiencies, and molecular diagnostics are uneven. Future research: Prioritize rodent biomonitoring, harmonized surveillance, improved molecular testing, and locally calibrated early‑warning systems for endemic hantaviruses.

papers.title: Hantavirus infection in emergency radiology: Imaging manifestations, pathophysiology, and infection control considerations.
papers.abstract: In April 2026, several cases of severe respiratory illnesses were reported aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius during its voyage from Argentina. Subsequent laboratory testing identified Andes virus (ANDV), a hantavirus subtype, with rare but documented human-to-human transmission. Although hantavirus infections are uncommon, both hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) are associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Their rapid progression and potential need for intensive respiratory support continue to pose important challenges for emergency departments, intensive care units, and radiology services. Because pulmonary imaging findings often evolve quickly, radiologists play a critical role in early recognition and triage. This review provides an overview of the pathophysiology, imaging manifestations, and operational considerations relevant to hantavirus infection in emergency radiology practice.

analysis.background: Recent April 2026 outbreak of severe respiratory illness on cruise ship MV Hondius, identified as Andes virus, highlighted the need for radiology awareness.
analysis.main_directions: The review addresses hantavirus pathophysiology, imaging manifestations, and operational/infection‑control considerations for emergency radiology.
analysis.current_state: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, though uncommon, cause high morbidity and mortality; Andes virus can transmit between humans; pulmonary imaging changes rapidly, making radiologists pivotal for early triage.
analysis.gaps: The swift clinical deterioration creates challenges for emergency, ICU, and radiology services, and data on imaging evolution and optimal infection‑control practices remain limited.
analysis.future_research: Prospective studies to define characteristic imaging timelines, evaluate radiology‑driven triage algorithms, and develop standardized infection‑control protocols in emergency settings are needed.

analysis_zh.background: 2026年4月在邮轮MV Hondius上爆发的严重呼吸道疾病(标识为安第斯病毒)凸显了放射学意识的必要性。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述涉及汉坦病毒的病理生理、影像表现以及急诊放射学的运营/感染控制考虑因素。
analysis_zh.current_state: 汉坦病毒肺综合征和肾综合征出血热虽罕见,但导致高发病率和死亡率;安第斯病毒可在人际间传播;肺部影像变化迅速,使放射科医生在早期分诊中发挥关键作用。

papers.title: EPIZOOTIC AND EPIDEMIC SITUATION OF HANTAVIRUS INFECTION IN THE WORLD
papers.abstract: This review examines the current epidemiological and epizootic situation in natural foci of hantavirus diseases across various regions of the world. Today, hantavirus diseases represent a significant threat to the sanitary and epidemiological well-being of populations worldwide, capable of seriously complicating the epidemiological situation. Approximately 200,000 cases are registered worldwide annually, although the intensity and dynamics of morbidity vary considerably across regions. In China — the country with the highest annual number of cases in the world — the overall incidence trend is declining. Ukraine is a natural endemic focus for the spread of hantaviruses that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). Given climate change, which stimulates rodent migration and reproduction, epidemiological risks for the rural population and military personnel are increasing. Data on the spread of hantavirus infection in the regions of Southeast Asia and the African continent require further study; however, it is quite evident that hantavirus infection is an underestimated public health problem in these regions, and its true scale — given the wide distribution of reservoir hosts — may be considerably greater than currently known. Keywords: hantavirus diseases, hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, epidemiological situation, natural reservoirs, pathogens.

analysis.background: A1 reviews the global epidemiological and epizootic situation of hantavirus diseases, highlighting their relevance to public health.
analysis.main_directions: A2 notes hantaviruses as a significant worldwide health threat; A6 links climate‑driven rodent dynamics to rising risk for rural and military populations; A7‑A8 point to insufficient data in Southeast Asia and Africa.
analysis.current_state: A3 reports ~200,000 annual cases with regional variability; A4 shows a declining incidence trend in China despite high case numbers; A5 identifies Ukraine as an endemic focus for HFRS.
analysis.gaps: A7 and A8 emphasize the paucity of surveillance data in Southeast Asia and Africa, suggesting substantial under‑recognition of disease burden.
analysis.future_research: A7‑A8 call for expanded epidemiological studies and surveillance in under‑studied regions, while A6 suggests research on climate‑change impacts on rodent reservoirs and associated human risk.

analysis.summary_en: Background: A1 reviews the global hantavirus epidemiology. Main directions: A2 highlights the worldwide health threat, A6 links climate‑driven rodent changes to rising risk, and A7‑A8 note data gaps in SE Asia and Africa. Current state: A3 cites ~200,000 annual cases with regional variation, A4 reports declining trends in China, and A5 marks Ukraine as an HFRS endemic focus. Gaps: A7‑A8 reveal limited surveillance in SE Asia and Africa, likely underestimating burden. Future research: A7‑A8 recommend expanded surveillance in these regions, and A6 urges studies on climate impacts on reservoirs and human exposure.

papers.title: Multi-Country Human-to-Human Andes Virus Outbreak on a Cruise Ship: A Disaster Report on Prehospital, Health Care Facility, and Public Health System Challenges - Essential Knowledge for Frontline Clinicians.
papers.abstract: Abstract The Andes Virus (ANDV) outbreak reported on May 2, 2026, aboard a luxury vessel departing from Ushuaia, Patagonia, Argentina, was caused by an Orthohantavirus unique in its person-to-person transmissibility in contrast to zoonotic transmission characteristic of better-known hantaviruses. Containment required coordinated international management because passengers and crew embarked and disembarked at several international ports-of-call prior to outbreak recognition, resulting in cross-border transmission potential. Among those who disembarked, several traveled on flights to various destinations. Cases subsequently manifested in multiple countries, including Tristan da Cunha, Spain, France, Switzerland, South Africa, Canada, and The Netherlands. Upon notification, international health authorities implemented containment measures, such as contact tracing, quarantine, and isolation. Uniquely, ANDV poses distinctive risks due to its immediately prodromal presymptomatic transmission potential, initial non-specific flu-like symptoms, prolonged incubation period, conceivable long-term neurologic and endocrinologic sequalae, high case fatality rates (CFRs), and possibility of international dissemination. This report describes the successful management of a multi-national outbreak associated with cruise-ship travel, a setting with unique challenges. It also examines implications and challenges for prehospital, health care facility, and public health systems for future ANDV outbreaks. The event was characterized by delayed recognition, international spread, and complex coordination across multiple jurisdictions and sectors, including medical and public health authorities, policy- and decision-makers, crisis and emergency risk-communication experts, media, logistics, transportation, and security. Rapid implementation of public health measures coupled with clinician implementation of the Identify-Isolate-Inform (3I) model, a clinical framework to detect and prevent the spread of infectious disease, at the prehospital and health care facility levels are critical actions that can contain future ANDV outbreaks.

This report describes the successful management of a multi-national outbreak associated with cruise-ship travel, a setting with unique challenges. It also examines implications and challenges for prehospital, health care facility, and public health systems for future ANDV outbreaks. The event was characterized by delayed recognition, international spread, and complex coordination across multiple jurisdictions and sectors, including medical and public health authorities, policy- and decision-makers, crisis and emergency risk-communication experts, media, logistics, transportation, and security. Rapid implementation of public health measures coupled with clinician implementation of the Identify-Isolate-Inform (3I) model, a clinical framework to detect and prevent the spread of infectious disease, at the prehospital and health care facility levels are critical actions that can contain future ANDV outbreaks.

The ship set sail on April 1, 2026 from Ushuaia, Patagonia, an area endemic for Orthohantavirus andesense, or Andes Virus (ANDV). Orthohantavirus are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded ribonucleic acid (RNA) viruses maintained primarily in rodent reservoirs; related hantaviruses have also been identified in bats and other small mammals. A significant number of individuals on the ship disembarked and traveled to various international destinations prior to awareness that they had been exposed to an infectious disease on board (Table 1). By the conclusion of the outbreak, there were a total of 13 cases (12 confirmed and one probable for ANDV). Overall, ten people recovered and three died, including https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1049023X26109108 Downloaded from https://www.cambridge.org/core. IP address: 57.151.137.182, on 04 Oct 2026 at 00:49:13, subject to the Cambridge Core terms of use, available at the index case.2 Confirmed cases were managed in several coun- tries: South Africa, the Canary Islands, the Netherlands, Switzerland, France, Canada, and Tristan da Cunha (UK territory) (Figure 1).3 No rodents were aboard the ship,4 indicating person-to-person viral spread.5 While the situation is novel, the agent is not. Prospective data show that ANDV produces systemic viremia and shedding of infectious virus in oral and respiratory fluids.6 Outbreak genomic analyses support that this shedding can translate into limited person-to-person transmission in close- contact settings.5 There are no licensed antivirals or vaccines. Unlike other Orthohantavirus species (Table 2), ANDV creates enough viremia in human body fluids to allow for limited human- to-human transmission.7,8 Infected individuals who travel inter- nationally or remain in confined settings can drive chains of transmission that pose serious global health security and One Health concerns with potential for wide dissemination and major health and socioeconomic impacts. According to data from the vessel’s operator, Oceanwide Expeditions (Vlissingen, The Netherlands), least 33 passengers from 12 nations (Canada, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Singapore, Sweden, Switzerland, Türkiye, the UK, and the United States) disembarked the MV Hondius at St. Helena, a British island in the South Atlantic, between April 21-24.9 Other scientific publications cite slightly different numbers,10 highlighting the challenges with data collection and effective communication during a rapidly evolving outbreak. On April 25, most of those who left the ship traveled together on the only commercial flight out of St. Helena, landing in Johannesburg, South Africa later that day. From there, most continued onward to other world-wide destinations. United States residents returned to five different states (Arizona, California, Georgia, Texas, and Virginia), each with its own health authority. All these passengers traveled unmonitored while potentially infectious (Figure 1). While data are inconclusive, WHO endorses the working hypothesis that the index patient was infected before boarding the ship in Ushuaia on April 1, likely through zoonotic exposure to ANDV in Patagonia. A New England Journal of Medicine article published on May 20, 2026 reported he developed symptoms on approximately April 3.11 Given the typical incubation period of two to six weeks, this strongly supports the theory that infection was not acquired on the ship. His condition deteriorated rapidly, and he died onboard ten days after departure. His body was removed 13 days later in St. Helena. The second case, the wife of the index case, was a passenger on the flight from St. Helena to O.R. Tambo International Airport in Johannesburg, South Africa. She had symptoms prior to boarding,2 transferred to another flight bound for the Netherlands, but dis- embarked prior to takeoff. Subsequently, she collapsed at the Table 1. A flight attendant, who had not been on the ship, reported to hospital in the Netherlands with symptoms suggestive of hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS; also known as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, or HPS). While the flight attendant tested negative for ANDV on both polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and antibody tests, her symptoms raised concern for secondary transmission. This illustrates the importance of prehospital, health care facility, and public health system pre- paredness to rapidly identify and isolate potentially infectious patients until the cause of their symptoms can be determined. Between May 4-5, three symptomatic passengers were medically evacuated from the ship to the Netherlands. The team consisted of two public health experts from WHO and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC; Solna, Sweden) for situation assessment, and two Dutch medical experts for clinical assessment and management. After anchoring at Tenerife, Canary Islands, 85 passengers and 35 crew disembarked for immediate medical evacuation and repa- triation. Asymptomatic Spanish nationals were transported to a military facility in Madrid, Spain, and the others to their countries of origin. The WHO recommended that all remain in prolonged quarantine (42 days). The WHO asked countries with repatriated nationals to initiate precautionary contact tracing. Persons were categorized as high risk (placed in quarantine) or low risk (performed active self- monitoring) continuing for 42 days following last known exposure.12 Source The investigators obtained clinical and treatment data exclusively from publicly available sources, such as peer-reviewed literature and aggregate event descriptions. Limitations to this methodology are highlighted by the lack of comprehensive individual-level data, including contact-tracing details. papers.title: Of mice and men: Updates on hantavirus disease and diagnostics.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are a diverse and widespread group of zoonotic viruses under the Orthohantavirus genus that can cause severe acute cardiopulmonary or renal disease. Hantavirus species are grouped generally as either New World or Old World based on geographic distribution, which is influenced by their respective host reservoir including rodents. Although there is no specific treatment for hantaviruses, recognizing clinical presentation and interpreting laboratory results for case identification can improve patient management. Here we review the epidemiology, clinical manifestations, and diagnostic testing options for hantavirus infection.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical virology : the official publication of the Pan American Society for Clinical Virology

papers.title: Andes Virus - A Clinical Review.
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) is the sole orthohantavirus with documented human-to-human transmission. We summarize the epidemiology and clinical features of ANDV infection and review best practices in clinical management, as based on published expert consensus guidelines, field experience, and clinical trials. We also evaluate currently available and investigational treatments (including the use of antiviral agents), assess emerging monoclonal antibody therapies, and outline prospects for vaccine development. Finally, we discuss important infection prevention and control measures.
papers.journal: The New England journal of medicine

papers.title: Hantavirus Infection Beyond the Lung: A Multi-Organ Radiological Perspective on Diagnosis, Imaging Modalities, and Precautionary Measures for Radiology Departments.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonotic disease with worldwide relevance, associated with significant morbidity and mortality through hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome. After recent reports, including a cluster of severe cases reported to the World Health Organization in 2026, increasing attention has been directed toward its clinical, pathological, and radiological spectrum. Radiology departments, as one of the most important health care providers involved in imaging for disease confirmation, detection of complications, and assessment of involvement of different body organs, should be familiar with the manifestations of suspected patients, the most appropriate imaging requests, and the precautionary measures required within the department to prevent disease transmission to both health care personnel and other patients undergoing imaging procedures. Therefore, in this review, we aimed to present recent clinical and radiological findings, as well as precautionary interventions that should be implemented in radiology departments.
papers.journal: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonotic disease with worldwide relevance, causing hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and associated with significant morbidity and mortality. (A1)
analysis.main_directions: Recent WHO-reported clusters in 2026 have increased attention on the clinical, pathological, and radiological spectrum, prompting a review of multi‑organ imaging findings and departmental precautionary measures. (A2)
analysis.current_state: Radiology departments are central to confirming infection, detecting complications, and assessing multi‑organ involvement, and must be familiar with appropriate imaging requests and safety protocols. (A3)
analysis.gaps: The abstract does not detail optimal imaging modalities for each organ, nor provide data on the efficacy of specific precautionary interventions, leaving best‑practice guidance uncertain.
analysis.future_research: Research should compare diagnostic performance of CT, MRI, and ultrasound for hantavirus‑related organ lesions and evaluate infection‑control strategies within radiology workflows.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is an emerging zoonosis causing severe pulmonary and renal syndromes with high morbidity/mortality (A1). Main directions: 2026 WHO clusters have spurred focus on its clinical, pathological, and radiological spectrum and on radiology department precautions (A2). Current state: Radiology is key for diagnosis, complication detection, and multi‑organ assessment, requiring appropriate imaging requests and safety measures (A3). Gaps: Optimal imaging modalities per organ and the effectiveness of precautionary measures are not defined. Future research: Comparative studies of CT, MRI, ultrasound for organ involvement and evaluation of infection‑control protocols in radiology are needed.

papers.title: Beyond the Kidney and Lung: Cutaneous and Mucosal Clues to Human Hantavirus Disease.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses that cause two overlapping vascular syndromes in humans: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including nephropathia epidemica, and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome. Although dermatologists are rarely central to hantavirus care, early visible abnormalities may occur on the skin, mucosa, and ocular surface. This narrative review synthesizes the dermatologic and mucocutaneous manifestations of human hantavirus disease, with emphasis on signs that should prompt diagnostic suspicion in dermatology, emergency, travel-medicine, and infectious-disease settings. The dermatologic signal is strongest in hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, where facial or upper-torso flushing, conjunctival and pharyngeal injection, petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, and mucosal bleeding may appear during the febrile or hemorrhagic phases. These findings are not pathognomonic, but their diagnostic value increases when they occur with rodent or outbreak exposure, thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy, and renal abnormalities such as proteinuria, hematuria, or acute kidney injury. In hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome, particularly infections caused by New World hantaviruses, visible cutaneous involvement is less prominent and may be absent despite severe pulmonary endothelial disease. We propose a practical dermatology-oriented trigger for suspicion based on exposure history, abrupt febrile illness, nephro-pulmonary involvement, thrombocytopenia, and vascular mucocutaneous findings. Hantavirus should be considered when otherwise unexplained vascular skin or mucosal signs occur in a febrile patient with thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, hypoxemia, or compatible exposure. The skin rarely diagnoses hantavirus alone, but it may shorten time to testing, supportive care, and public-health notification.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome, prompting interest in non‑renal/lung manifestations.
analysis.main_directions: The review highlights dermatologic and mucocutaneous signs as early clues, outlines exposure‑related diagnostic triggers, and discusses differences between HFRS and HPS presentations.
analysis.current_state: Facial flushing, conjunctival injection, petechiae, purpura, and mucosal bleeding are well‑documented in HFRS, whereas cutaneous involvement is often absent in New World HPS.
analysis.gaps: Skin findings are not pathognomonic and their diagnostic utility depends on concurrent exposure, thrombocytopenia, and renal signs; data on prevalence and specificity remain limited.
analysis.future_research: Prospective validation of dermatology‑oriented suspicion algorithms and systematic surveillance of mucocutaneous manifestations across hantavirus strains are needed.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause renal and pulmonary vascular syndromes, raising interest in skin clues. Main directions: The review surveys dermatologic/mucosal signs, exposure‑based triggers, and contrasts HFRS vs HPS. Current state: Classic vascular skin findings are common in HFRS but often absent in New World HPS. Gaps: Skin signs lack specificity and data on their prevalence are sparse. Future research: Validate dermatology‑focused diagnostic algorithms and conduct systematic surveillance of mucocutaneous manifestations across hantavirus species.

papers.title_zh: 超越肾脏和肺部:人类汉坦病毒疾病的皮肤和黏膜线索。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒是啮齿动物传播的病毒,可导致肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒肺/心肺综合征,因而引起对非肾/肺表现的关注。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述强调皮肤和黏膜表现作为早期线索,概述与暴露相关的诊断触发因素,并讨论肾综合征出血热与汉坦病毒肺综合征的临床表现差异。
analysis_zh.current_state: 面部潮红、结膜充血、出血点、紫癜和黏膜出血在肾综合征出血热中有充分记录,而在新世界汉坦病毒肺综合征中皮肤累及常缺失。
analysis_zh.gaps: 皮肤表现并非特异性,其诊断价值取决于同时存在的暴露史、血小板减少和肾脏体征;关于其患病率和特异性的资料仍有限。
analysis_zh.future_research: 需要前瞻性验证以皮肤学为导向的疑诊算法,并系统监测不同汉坦病毒株系的黏膜皮肤表现。
